4.44.m:
Skanda said: / Then, Hara, the lord of the universe, residing in a jeweled palace of peerless brilliance shining within the caves of Mount Mandara, / surrounded on all sides by the gods, and clothing the sky with his own peaks— / he, charming with a slender digit of the moon, / the author of peace, did not find happiness, burning with fever born of separation from expanding Kāśī. / The paste of Malaya-born sandalwood, applied even by the foe of Tripura to cool the fire of separation, / now truly assumed a burning thirst.
The soft [lotus-stalks] of lotus ponds that remove burning heat were turned into bracelets;
when they were pronounced by the Lord to be snakes, they became truly so—ah, the will of the Great Lord!
The full moon, soft essence churned from the ocean of milk and extracted by the gods,
became emaciated, its body dissolving under the heat radiating from the head of the Lord, burned by separation.
Because Hara, afflicted with burning pain, held the celestial river
which removes anguish in the broad corner of the bower of his matted hair, he does not release it even now.

4.44.m:
Śaṃkara, master of his senses, was forcibly brought under the power of that great longing of separation;
he sat despondent among the assembled gods, enveloped by intense torment.
It is an exceedingly wondrous thing that though he is himself the pure fire,
the lord of the three worlds was scorched by the fire born of separation from his own city.
He who continually adorns his forehead with a digit of the moon—
that very moon, quite contrarily, burned even that Lord.
Poison glistens in the region of his throat, yet he was not tormented by that;
wondrously, he was tormented only by the clusters of cold rays of the nectar-rayed [moon]!
To remove that anguish of separation with splashes of gleaming water mixed with yellow sandalwood,
his heart burned even from that, but not from the fiery breaths arising from the hoods of expanding serpents.
Hara destroys every delusion arising from the false notion of a snake in a garland and the like;
wondrous it is that in his case, even on a real garland, the delusion arose that it was a great snake!
Though he completely removes the threefold torment even when merely brought into the path of memory,

4.44.m:
the Unborn himself, tormented by separation from Kāśī, spoke somewhat to himself:
“If only the breeze coming from Kāśī would embrace my limbs,
then my burning torment would find peace; it does not do so even by immersion in Lake Mānasa!
Alas, how would that burning torment have subsided which was fostered by Dakṣa's daughter,
if the daughter of the Himālaya had not swiftly become a life-giving creeper for me?
Dakṣa's daughter, passing away when abandoning her body, did not cause my mind to suffer
as it burns intensely with this immense heat born of separation from Avimukta!
O Kāśī, when shall I joyfully attain again the happiness born of embracing you,
by which my wonderful limbs will immediately become cooled?
O Kāśī, destroyer of multitudes of sins, the fire born of separation from you,
wondrously flares up with the gentle nectar streams of the moon's digit as if with clarified butter!
Formerly, my burning pain born of separation from Dakṣa's daughter vanished through the medicine that was the daughter of the Himālaya;
now, indeed, I shall by no means attain peace unless I quickly behold Kāśī!”

4.44.m:
Reciting thus in his mind, Śiva, entirely concealing the outward signs of his torment,
was somehow perceived as separated [from his beloved] by the Mother of the World, the mother of intellects. // 4.1.44.20
Though she formed half his body, she did not know the cause of his longing;
he, the destroyer of the burning distress of bowed living beings, was addressed with words by his beloved: // 21
Śrī Pārvatī said:
“O omnipresent one, everything is in your hand! What separation can there be for you, whose yoga shines forth?
Ah, your ashes grant prosperity; though she bears the shoots of every misfortune, the earth bears all creatures! // 22
O Lord, through not beholding you, the worlds instantly go to ruin like something pitiful.
Even an ordinary person cast out from your fraction of grace was once affirmed by you with ‘Om’. // 23
The moon, the sun, and fire do not cause you distress,
since, O three-eyed one, they are your eyes; and your beloved [Gaṅgā] of sparkling water rests on your crest. // 24
These serpents of yours never bite, and poison does not spread [in you], O blue-throated one!
And I, O Vāmadeva, am the fair woman making up your left side, united with your mind. // 25 //”

When this beneficial speech was thus spoken by the mother of the seeds of cyclic existence,
Giriśa took up speech to reply to that weaving of words. // 26
The Lord said:
“Ah, Kāśī!” Saying this, Bhava, who possesses the eight forms, manifested the eight emotions.
Quickly Śivā realized: “Surely Hara has been captivated by Kāśī!” // 27
Then, having the creepers of that forest as her childhood companions, Śivā introduced the topic of that forsaken city which bestows liberation. // 28
Pārvatī said:
“Let us go, O Bhava, destroyer of Smara, to the city of Kāśī, / held aloft upon your trident even during the cosmic dissolution when the waters meet the vault of heaven,
which displays the beauty of a white lotus! // 29

Are there not here thousands of cities, grounds of all prosperity at every step?

Entering the sky, with a speed greater even than thought,
those Yoginīs went along, speaking to one another with joy:
“Today we are exceedingly fortunate, since by the God of gods himself,
favored, we have been dispatched to the glorious Ānandakānana.
Today, all at once, two great gains, not easily attained, have occurred:
honor from the King with the Three Eyes, and the sight of Kāśī.”
Thus, with joyful minds, that host of Yoginīs, leaving the bower of Mount Mandara
and quickening their speed of flight in the sky, made that city a guest of their eyes.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, named 'The Description of Kāśī,' in the first half of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa, in the glorious Skanda Mahāpurāṇa consisting of eighty-one thousand verses.

4.45.m: Skanda said:
Then that host of Yoginīs, casting its gaze from afar,
praised the creation of the long reach of their eyes as fruitful.
The flags of the celestial rows of palaces, with fluttering banner-cloths,
seemed to respectfully summon travelers standing afar on the road.
By the flashing rubies of the palaces, their rays expanding,
the sky, though deep blue, was seen as exceedingly bright.
Concealing their divine nature through illusion and assuming the attire suited to pilgrims,
the circle of Yoginīs entered Kāśī without distinct order.
